en: I worship the state of Rāmacandra, which is to be known through the Muktikopaniṣad and which embodies the intent of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
Hari Om. That is fullness; this is fullness. From fullness, fullness arises.
When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ. In the delightful city of Ayodhyā, in the center of a pavilion of jewels, [he is] accompanied by Sītā, Bharata, Saumitri, Śatrughna, and others. || 1 ||
He was being praised day and night by hosts of sages beginning with Sanaka, by those beginning with Vasiṣṭha, by those beginning with Śuka, and by other devotees as well.
At the conclusion of his meditative absorption, he beheld Hari, the witness of thousands of mental transformations, the changeless one, who is ever intent upon meditation on His own true nature.
Praising Rāma with devotion and service, the son of the Wind-god (Hanumān) asked:
"O Rāma, you are the Supreme Self, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (4)
Now, O best of the Raghus, I bow to you again and again;
O Rāma, I desire to know your true form in its essential reality for the sake of liberation. || 5 ||
O Rāma, out of compassion, tell me that by which I may be liberated from the bondage of existence without effort, so that I may become free.
"Well asked, O mighty-armed one! I shall speak; listen to it according to the truth.
I am firmly established in the Vedānta; take refuge in the Vedānta. (7)
"O best of the Raghus, what are the Vedāntas and where do they exist? Tell me.
"Hanumān, listen; I shall explain the nature of the Vedāntas succinctly."
The Vedas, very extensive, were born from Viṣṇu as my very breath;
the Vedānta is firmly established within the Veda, like oil in sesame seeds.
O Rāma, descendant of Raghu, how many kinds of Vedas are there, and what are their branches? Among them, which are the Upaniṣads? Please tell me this according to the truth.
Śrī Rāma said: The Vedas are declared to be fourfold through the divisions beginning with the Ṛgveda;
they indeed have many branches, and within those are likewise the Upaniṣads.
The branches of the Ṛgveda are twenty-one in number;
O son of the Maruts, there are one hundred and nine branches of the Yajurveda.
O scorcher of foes, the branches of the Sāman have arisen in the number of a thousand;
O Hari, the branches of the Atharvaṇa consist of fifty divisions.
For each branch, one Upaniṣad is prescribed;
and whoever recites even a single verse from among them with devotion toward me, [attains the fruit]. (14)
He attains the state of union with me, which is difficult even for sages to obtain.
O Rāma, some of the best of sages have declared that liberation is one alone. (15)
Some [attained liberation] through the recitation of your name in Kāśī by means of the instruction of Tāra;
others through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and still others through the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga).
Other supreme sages, through their investigation into the meaning of the Vedānta texts, have declared that liberation is fourfold, categorized as sālokya and so forth. (17)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O monkey, whether one is devoted to evil conduct or not, through the worship of my name alone, there is but one liberation—Kaivalya—which is the ultimate reality. (18)
One attains liberation as *sālokya* (residing in the same world), but not [merely] another world and so forth;
however, one who dies here at the Brahma-nāla in Kāśī shall attain the state of being the Self (Brahman).
A human being attains liberation from which there is no return;
whether one dies anywhere else or in Kāśī, such a person becomes Maheśvara.
One should impart the instruction regarding Me into the right ear of the living being;
with the entire flood of sins shaken off, he attains similarity to My own form.
That very state is designated as liberation characterized by residence in the same world (sālokya) and having the same form (sārūpya).
Having become devoted to virtuous conduct, the twice-born man should always remain with his mind focused on nothing else.

When this state of being, which consists of my entire self, attains proximity to me, that very state is considered liberation consisting of residence in the same world (sālokya), having the same form (sārūpya), and proximity (sāmīpya). || 23 ||
Meditating upon my imperishable quality by the path taught by the Guru,
the twice-born man shall properly attain union with me, like a bee and its larva.
That itself shall be the liberation of union (sāyujya-mukti), auspicious and bestowing the bliss of Brahman;
indeed, the fourfold liberation that arises through my worship—|| 25 ||
By what means is this liberation as absolute isolation (kaivalya) accomplished?
For those seeking liberation, the Māṇḍūkya alone is sufficient for their release. (26)
Nevertheless, if knowledge is not yet established for you, study the ten Upaniṣads;
having attained knowledge, you shall go to my own abode before long.
Nevertheless, O son of Añjanā, if there is no firmness in your knowledge,
then master the Upaniṣad known as the Dvātriṃśat and turn back [from this path].
O Videhamukta, if you have this desire, recite [this] one hundred and eight times;
listen to their sequence and their pacification, which I shall explain according to the truth. (29)
The Īśa, Kaṭha, Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, and Taittirīya; likewise the Aitareya, Chāndogya, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka. (1.30)
The Brahmakaivalya, Jābāla, Śvetāśvatara, Haṃsa, Āruṇi, Garbha, Nārāyaṇa, Haṃsa, Bindu, Nāda, Śiras, and Śikhā. || 31 ||
The Maitrāyaṇī, Kauṣītakī, Bṛhajjābāla, Tāpanī, Kālāgnirudra, Maitreyī, Subāla, Kṣurika, and Mantrikā [Upaniṣads]. || 32 ||
The *Vajrasūcika*, the secret essence of all, which is without support,
awakens the self through the reality of yoga, the science of meditation on the *tejas* and *nāda*.
The wandering ascetic Triśikhī, Sītā, Cūḍā, Nirvāṇamaṇḍala, Dakṣiṇā, Śarabha, Skanda, and the one called Mahānārāyaṇa. 34.
The Rahasya, Rāmatapana, Vāsudeva, Mudgala, Śāṇḍilya, Paiṅgala, Bhikṣu, Mahacchārīraka, and Śikhā. (35)
The rosary is the renunciant who has transcended the fourth state (turiyatita);
the single unmanifest syllable is the full [vessel]; and the water-pot is the internal self (adhyatma) of the sun-eyed one. || 36 ||

The Sāvitrī-ātman, the Pāśupata, the Supreme Brahman, the Avadhūtaka; the Tripurātapana, the Goddess Tripurā, and the Kaṭha-bhāvanā; the Heart, Kuṇḍalinī, the sacred ash, and the vision of the multitude of Rudrākṣas. || 37 ||
The Tārasāra Mahāvākya, the Pañcabrahma Agnihotra,
the Gopālatāpana, the Kṛṣṇa, the Yājñavalkya, and the Varāhaka [Upaniṣads].
The Śāṭyāyanī, Hayagrīva, Dattātreya, Gāruḍa,
Kalijābāli, Saubhāgyarahasya, Ṛcamuktikā, || 39 ||
Thus, this one hundred and eight [verses] destroys the three types of mental cultivation;
it bestows knowledge and dispassion upon men and eliminates the three types of latent impressions.
Preceded by the respective pacification rites prescribed for the northeast,
[he should receive it] directly from the mouth of the preceptor who has bathed after completing his vows of Vedic learning.
Those best of the twice-born who, having taken up [this work], recite it one hundred and eight times,
become liberated while living until the exhaustion of their prārabdha karma.
Then, when the *prārabdha* has reached its end solely through the power of time, my Vaidehīs attain liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (43)
Among all the Upaniṣads, this one hundred and eight [verses] is the essence;
by merely hearing it once, the multitude of all sins is destroyed. (44)
O son of the Wind, this secret scripture consisting of one hundred and eight [verses] has been taught by me to you, my disciple. (45)
Whether read with knowledge or even without knowledge, it grants liberation from bondage to those who recite it;
to one who asks, a kingdom should be given, wealth should be given, and every desire should be fulfilled.
This [text] consisting of one hundred and eight [verses] must not be given to just anyone;
it should certainly not be given to an atheist, to an ungrateful person, or to one who delights in wicked conduct.
It should never be given to one who is averse to devotion to Me, nor to one who is deluded by the pitfalls of the scriptures, nor to one who is devoid of devotion to the Guru. 48.
To Māruti, who was devoted to service, a beneficial son, my devotee, of virtuous character, of noble birth, and of excellent intellect; (49)
Having examined it thoroughly, this one hundred and eight [verses] should indeed be given.
Whoever recites or even hears it attains me; of this there is no doubt. This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Knowledge came to the Brāhmaṇa, saying: 'Guard me, for I am your treasure.'"
Do not speak this to one who is censorious, dishonest, or deceitful; let it not be so for me, that I may remain possessed of vigor.

Only to one who knows, who has heard the scriptures, who is vigilant, wise, and endowed with celibacy—to such a person who has approached you, having thoroughly examined him, you should indeed impart this Vaiṣṇava realization centered on the Self. 1.
Then Māruti questioned Śrī Rāmacandra, saying,
"Please recite the Śānti mantras separately according to the divisions of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas.
Śrī Rāma replied as follows.
Of the ten Upaniṣads belonging to the Ṛgveda— namely, the Aitareya, Kauṣītaki, Nādabindu, Ātmaprabodha, Nirvāṇa, Mudgala, Akṣamālikā, Tripurā, Saubhāgya, and Bahvṛca.
"May my speech be in my mind"—this is the peace invocation. || 1 ||
The Īśāvāsya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Jābāla, Haṃsa, Paramahaṃsa, Subāla, Mantrikā, Nirālamba, Triśikhībrāhmaṇa, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, Advayatāraka,
Paiṅgala, Bhikṣu, Turīyātīta, Adhyātma, Tārasāra, and Yājñavalkya [Upaniṣads].
The peace invocation for the nineteen Upanishads belonging to the Śāṭyāyanīya recension of the Śukla Yajurveda is: "Fullness is this. (2)
The Kaṭhavallī, Taittirīyaka, Brahmakaivalya, Śvetāśvatara, Garbha, Nārāyaṇa, Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kālāgnirudra, Kṣurikā, Sarvasāra, Śukarahasya, Tejobindu, Dhyānabindu, and Brahmavidyā Upaniṣads.
Of the Yogatattva, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Skanda, Śārīraka, Yogaśikhā, Ekākṣara, Akṣi, Avadhūta, Kaṭharudra, Hṛdaya, Yogakuṇḍalinī, Pañcabrahma,
Prāṇāgnihotra, Varāha, Kalisantaraṇa, and Sarasvatīrahasya [Upaniṣads].
May he protect us both—this is the peace-chant for the thirty-two Upanishads contained within the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 3.

And of the sixteen [Upanishads] belonging to the Sāmaveda: the Kenopaniṣad, Chāndogya, Āruṇi, Maitrāyaṇī, Maitreyī, Vajrasūcika, Yogacūḍāmaṇi, Vāsudeva, Mahatsaṃnyāsa, Avyakta, Kuṇḍikā, Sāvitrī, Rudrākṣa, Jābāladarśana, Jābālī, and [the rest].
May the Upanishads be nourished; thus, peace. 4.
The Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Atharvaśiras, Atharvaśikhā, Bṛhajjābāla,
Nṛsiṃhatāpanī, Nāradaparivrājaka, Sītāśarabha, Mahānārāyaṇa,
Rāmarahasya, Rāmatāpanī, Śāṇḍilya, and Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka Upaniṣads.
The meditations on the thirty-one [deities] belonging to the Atharvaveda: Annapūrṇā, Sūrya, Ātman, Pāśupata, Parabrahman,
Tripurātapanadevī, Brahman, Jābāla, Gaṇapati, Mahāvākya, Gopālatāpana, Kṛṣṇa, Hayagrīva,
Dattātreya, and Gāruḍa.
The peace invocation for the Mupaniṣads: "May there be blessing for our ears. || 5 ||

Men desiring liberation, endowed with the fourfold qualifications and possessed of faith, [should seek] a true Guru who is born of a noble family, learned in the Vedas, affectionate toward the scriptures, virtuous, straightforward, devoted to the welfare of all beings, and an ocean of compassion.

Having approached according to the prescribed rite with offerings in hand, having studied the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads according to the rules, and having performed hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana) without interruption, they—
upon the exhaustion of their prārabdha karma and the dissolution of the three bodies— became liberated from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
The state of being as full as the space within a jar is disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*). That alone is called absolute liberation (*kaivalyamukti*).

For this very reason, even those residing in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) attain absolute liberation together with him after having performed such acts as hearing the Vedānta from the mouth of Brahmā. Therefore, it is said that for all beings, absolute liberation is attained through knowledge alone.
"Not by ritual action, nor by enumeration, nor by yoga, nor by meditation, etc."—thus says the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||
Thus, Māruti questioned Śrī Rāmacandra:
"What is this perfection (*siddhi*), and what is the purpose of that perfection?
Śrī Rāma replied: "It is the [cessation of] a person's state of being an agent and an enjoyer."
The mental state characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, being of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*), constitutes bondage.

The cessation thereof is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Upon the exhaustion of the momentum of past actions (*prārabdha-karma*), one who is freed from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) attains disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), like the space within a jar [when the jar is broken].
The one hundred and eight Upaniṣads are the authoritative source for both liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*).
The purpose is the attainment of eternal bliss by means of the cessation of suffering such as agency and the like;
this is to be accomplished through human effort, just as [the goal of a son is attained] through the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice.
Through trade and other such means, one acquires wealth; through the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, heaven;

and likewise, through the attainment of samādhi produced by hearing the Vedānta and other practices accomplished by human effort, there is the attainment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) and so forth. This attainment results from the destruction of all latent impressions (vāsanās).
In this regard, there are these verses:
Human effort is considered to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
Among these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal.
Due to the latent impression of worldly life, the latent impression of scriptural learning, and the latent impression of the body, knowledge does not arise in its true form for a living being. (2)
The manifestation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is of two kinds: the auspicious and the inauspicious.
If you are led there by a flood of pure latent impressions, [then you shall attain liberation]. (3)
By that very sequence, may you swiftly attain my state;
yet, if an inauspicious disposition should entangle you in distress, [then act accordingly].
Therefore, O monkey, that former [mind] must be conquered by you with effort;
for the river of latent impressions flows along both auspicious and inauspicious paths.
One should apply human effort to direct [the mind] onto the auspicious path;
one should cause that which has entered into inauspicious states to descend into the auspicious alone.
Driven from the unwholesome it goes toward the wholesome, and from that, again, toward the other;
with human effort, one should cherish the child-like mind. (7)
O crusher of enemies, know that when, through the power of immediate practice, your latent impressions (vāsanā) arise, then you should recognize the success of that practice.
Even when there is doubt, practice that which is intensely auspicious;
for when auspicious latent impressions increase, O Son of the Wind, there is no fault.

O Mahāmati, the exhaustion of latent impressions, the [transformation of] consciousness, and the destruction of the manas—when practiced for a long time, these are considered to yield their fruit simultaneously. (2.10)
Thus, as long as these three are not practiced repeatedly in equal measure,
the attainment of the state does not occur even in hundreds of years.
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time,
they do not bestow accomplishment, just like mantras that have been merely recited.
When these three are practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without a doubt, like fibers from a lotus stalk when cut.
The false latent impression of saṃsāra, practiced throughout hundreds of previous births, is never extinguished anywhere except through the power of long-term cultivation. (14)
Therefore, O gentle one, with diligent human effort and discernment, having cast the desire for enjoyment far away, take refuge in these three alone. (15)

Therefore, the wise know that the mind joined with latent impressions (vāsanā) is bound; when it is completely abandoned of latent impressions, it is said to be liberated. O great monkey, quickly practice the state of the mind being free from latent impressions.
Through right discernment of the Truth, latent impressions (vāsanā) dissolve;
and upon the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind attains tranquility like a lamp [when its fuel is exhausted]. 17.
Having completely abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanā) within me, whose form is pure consciousness (cinmātra),
he who remains free from agitation is myself— consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccitsukhātmaka).

Whether he practices meditative absorption or performs actions—or whether he does not perform them—one whose every effort is taken up by the heart and who possesses the highest intention is indeed liberated. (19)

For one whose mind is free from latent impressions, there is no purpose served by inaction, nor is there any purpose served by ritual acts; nor is there any purpose served by means or the recitation of mantras. (2.20)
Apart from the silence resulting from the abandonment of latent impressions, there is no higher state.
Even though this sensory faculty, such as the eye, is devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), it functions spontaneously toward its own external object, having latent impressions alone as its cause.
Just as the eye falls upon objects within its range of vision without passion,
even though they are effortlessly presented to it, so too does the intellect of the wise man fall upon worldly affairs.
Sages know that the arising and ceasing of the mind, manifested as the consciousness of existence and corresponding to the vital breath (*māruta*), is *vāsanā*.
Through the persistent cultivation of the notion that objects of perception are real, the extremely fickle mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death. (25)
The vibration of the vital breath occurs by the power of latent impressions, and by that [vibration], latent impressions are produced;
thus, through this, there arises the sequence of seed and sprout for the seed of the mind. || 26 ||
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and latent impressions.
When one of these two is exhausted, both quickly perish. (27)
Due to the practice of non-attachment, due to the avoidance of the cultivation of worldly existence,
and due to the vision of the destruction of the body, latent impressions (vāsanā) do not arise.
Through the complete relinquishing of latent impressions, the mind (citta) attains the state of no-mind (acittatā).
When the mind, due to the constant absence of latent impressions (vāsanā), no longer perceives anything, then the state of no-mind (amanas-tā) arises,
which bestows supreme tranquility.
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not realized that supreme state, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. (2.30)
Therefore, since the impurities have been ripened and the reality has certainly been realized,
you, being free from affliction, must surely abandon even this auspicious flood of latent impressions.
The destruction of the mind is of two kinds: with form and indeed without form.
That which is with form belongs to the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta); that which is without form belongs to the one who has attained liberation from the body.
O Pāvana, now listen with respect to its destruction:
when that which is called the destruction of the mind occurs again, being endowed with qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it attains peace; of this there is no doubt. (33)
The mind of one liberated while living is completely freed from further birth.
This destruction of the mind with form belongs to one who is liberated while living;
however, the formless destruction of the mind leads to liberation as a disembodied spirit (vaidehī-mukti).
Possessing thousands of sprouts, branches, fruits, and foliage.
The root of this tree of saṃsāra is established in the mind;
I consider that it is indeed volition (saṃkalpa). Therefore, by the cessation of volition, that [tree] is destroyed.
Quickly dry it up so that the tree of saṃsāra withers;
there is only one means for this: the restraint of one's own mind. (38)
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great awakening.
The mind of the wise man goes to its destruction, for the mind is indeed the shackle of the knower.
Just as long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on the single reality, so long do latent impressions (vāsanās) dance about in the heart like Vetālas in the night. 2.40.
For one whose mental pride has perished and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses,
the latent tendencies for worldly enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter.
Pressing hand against hand, grinding tooth against tooth,
and crushing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind.
Sitting down again and again, even by one who reflects upon it repeatedly, the mind cannot be conquered without an irreproachable method. (43)
Just as a rutting, wicked elephant cannot be controlled without a goad, so too [the mind is not subdued] without the acquisition of the science of the self and association with the virtuous. (44)
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath—these indeed are the mature methods for conquering the mind. (45)
Those who, despite these methods being available, restrain the mind by force, are like those who cast away the lamp of consciousness and seek to dispel darkness with collyrium. (46)
Those deluded ones who strive to conquer the mind by force are like those who attempt to bind a furious lord of elephants with lotus fibers. (47)
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which sustains the creepers of its functions:
one is the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), and the second is firm conceptualization (bhāvanā). 48.
For that all-pervading consciousness is set in motion by the vibration of the vital breath;
since it is from one-pointedness of mind that knowledge is said to arise. (49)
Next, the meditation that accomplishes this is taught as it truly is:

even without the entire process of transformation, through the sequence of the reversal of manifestation, contemplate pure consciousness—consciousness and bliss—which is glory and the absence of misfortune. (2.50)
When the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart, that state which is experienced by yogis is known as kumbhaka. || 51 ||
When the prāṇa has gone outside and the apāna has not yet arisen, they know that state of full equilibrium existing externally to be the external kumbhaka. || 52 ||
The continuous flow of mental activity in the form of Brahman, devoid of ego-sense,
becomes samprajñāta-samādhi through the excellence of the practice of dhyāna.
The mind whose fluctuations have been stilled bestows supreme bliss;
this is the samādhi known as "asamprajñāta" (superconscious), which is dear to yogins.

Empty of radiance, empty of mind, and empty of intellect, yet consisting of consciousness—this is the samādhi cultivated by the sages, which takes the form of the exclusion of that which is not [the Self]. (55)
Filled above, filled below, and filled in the middle, it is of the nature of Śiva;
for this ultimate samādhi is indeed directly revealed by the mouth of Brahmā. 56.
That grasping of an object which, through firm cultivation, has abandoned all prior and subsequent deliberation, is proclaimed as *vāsanā*. (57)
O best of monkeys, that very state which he has cultivated within himself through intense spiritual urgency quickly becomes his own, as he is freed from all other latent impressions.
For when a person of such a nature, rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā), perceives this [world] as a real entity, he becomes utterly deluded. (59)
Due to the diversity of the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that [consciousness] does not abandon its own nature;
yet one of poor vision perceives it as deluded, just as one under the influence of intoxication [sees everything falsely]. (2.60)
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure. The impure is the cause of birth, while the pure is the destroyer of birth.
The wise declare that impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) is dense in form, consisting of thick ignorance, characterized by intense egoism, and the cause of rebirth;
yet, once the sprout of rebirth is abandoned, its persistence is like that of a parched seed. (62)
What is the use of this futile rumination on the patched garment of many scriptural discourses?
One must diligently seek the inner light within the wind. 63.
O tiger among monkeys, he who remains by himself in his own absolute nature, having abandoned both seeing and not-seeing— he is Brahman, and he is himself a knower of Brahman.
Having studied the four Vedas and the various scriptures many times over,
one who does not know the reality of Brahman is like a ladle that knows not the flavor of the food it stirs.
If a person is not repelled by the foul odor of the impurities of his own body, what other cause for detachment could possibly be taught to him? (66)
The body is exceedingly impure, while the embodied soul is utterly pure;
having understood the difference between these two, for which of them is purification prescribed? (67)
For one is bound by being bound to latent impressions (vāsanā), and liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
Having completely abandoned latent impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation.
Having first abandoned mental impressions of sense objects, take up the stainless impressions known as the impressions of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. (69)
Therefore, having renounced even these, and even while engaging with them,
remain inwardly peaceful, equal in affection toward all, and possessed of the latent impression of pure consciousness alone.
Then, having abandoned even that [mind] together with the intellect and the mental faculty,
O Māruti, remain fixed in me with your remaining steady concentration.
Soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless;
nameless and lineage-less— such is my form.
Worship him constantly, O destroyer of the distress of the son of the Wind-god.
The supreme nature of consciousness is like the sky, once-and-for-all manifest, unborn, one,
and imperishable; it is untainted, all-pervading, and non-dual.
And that very same thing, entirely liberated, I am—Oṃ.
But as for vision, I am pure and changeless by nature; no object belongs to me by my very essence,
whether in front, across, above, below, or anywhere at all.
Meditate here upon the thought: "I am the perfectly full ground. (74)
I am unborn and immortal, likewise ageless and deathless, self-luminous, all-pervading, and imperishable;
transcending both cause and effect, I am stainless.
Always contemplate here: "I am ever content."
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when his own body has been surrendered to time, he enters into disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
This very point has been expressed in a Ṛgvedic verse:
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky.
The wise, ever-vigilant, and inspired singers kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Om, "Truth," thus is the Upanishad. Om. That is full, this is full; from fullness, fullness arises.
When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Hariḥ Oṃ, that is the Truth.
Thus ends the Muktikopaniṣad.
